title: How Indigenous Restaurants Build Their Drink Menus
summary: Chefs contend with the history of industrialized alcohol—and the misconceptions and stigma around it—while designing their bar programs.
content:
When he opened his progressive Indigenous restaurant Naagan in Ontario, Canada, in late 2024, Ojibwe chef Zach Keeshig knew that he wouldn’t serve wine, beer or spirits. The alcohol-related death rate among Native people in North America remains three to five times higher than the general population’s—statistics that, for Keeshig, are hardly abstract. He’d seen many people close to him succumb to alcoholism. His own father had recently died, “sitting by himself, drinking.” Moreover, Keeshig wanted to “tell the story of what Indigenous food could be,” and like white flour, processed sugar and other ingredients he’d omitted from Naagan’s kitchen, alcohol was not part of the pre-contact Indigenous diet. For many North American Indigenous chefs, alcohol presents a conundrum: Bar programs are cash cows and it’s tough to run an upscale restaurant without one, but what kind of bar program makes sense in an Indigenous restaurant?

Let’s get this out of the way: The theory that Native peoples have some biological weakness to alcohol has been soundly debunked. Historically, that theory has functioned as a convenient blame-shifter, used as “proof” that Natives simply can’t hold their liquor, and that “the problems Natives face have nothing to do with settler violence,” says Michael D. Wise, author of Native Foods: Agriculture, Indigeneity, and Settler Colonialism in American History. “Alcohol is this deus ex machina force that absolves American settlers.” 

Although for millennia, Indigenous peoples brewed fermented drinks and ingested mind-altering substances, particularly in ceremony, it was European settlers and their descendants who industrialized alcohol, bringing beer to the Americas, introducing Vitis vinifera for wine and eventually distilling spirits. By the late 1800s, the federal governments of the United States and Canada had forced hundreds of thousands of Native people off their ancestral homelands, disrupted their food sovereignty and herded them onto reservations. Most Indigenous people today live in urban and suburban environments, but those who remain in tribal communities (about 20 percent in the United States and 40 percent in Canada) contend with a slew of alcohol-abuse risk factors, including remoteness, lack of resources, stigma and poverty. “Environments in which Native people live expose them to PTSD-qualifying events (death, threatened death, actual or threatened serious injury, or actual or threatened sexual violence) far more frequently than the environments of their non-Indian counterparts,” says Spero Manson, director of the Centers for American Indian & Alaska Native Health at Colorado School of Public Health. “We’re talking 60-70 percent of individuals living in tribal communities being exposed to serious trauma.”

In Indigenous restaurants, alcohol is not neutral, so some chefs serve it with caveats. “We don’t mix alcohol with medicine,” says Inez Cook of First Nations restaurant Salmon n’ Bannock in Vancouver, British Columbia. She reserves traditionally medicinal ingredients like sweetgrass and sage for mocktails. In cocktails, she showcases hard-to-come-by Indigenous ingredients, including soopolallie, or soap berries. When she can source soopolallie, she whips it into a foam to garnish a blend of orange juice, sparkling water, vodka and “Bella Coola tea” prepared with berries, rosehips, hibiscus and maple.

For Cree chef Shane Chartrand, dinners at his restaurant Paperbirch in Alberta, Canada, aren’t ceremonial. “There’s no smudging or land acknowledgement or anything,” he says. “This is just the culinary arts. It’s just dinner.” Because of that, though he’s sober himself, he feels comfortable offering local mead, beer and wine. He also acknowledges the demand for alcoholic beverages. “I can only be as Indigenous as the world allows me to be at a dinner where people are paying $120,” he says. Choctaw chef David Skinner of Ishtia in Kemah, Texas, concurs: “We don’t add alcohol to any of the food,” says, “but if you’re spending a couple hundred dollars and three hours of your life in a restaurant, you’re going to want a glass of wine or a cocktail.” 

It’s true that they are going to want it. But they also might act suspicious about it: Although Natives in the food and beverage space are expected to supply booze, doing so subjects them to stereotypes. As Chiricahua Apache Nde and Rarámuri brewer and distiller Roxanne Fernandez Tiburolobo put it, “I’ve had people that I brewed with be like, ‘Oh, you’re native? I didn’t know you people could have alcohol.’”

title: How to Use Génépy in Cocktails
summary: An updated guide to the bracing herbal liqueur, a close cousin of Chartreuse, which adds an alpine twist to any drink.
content:
Just five years ago, génépy (or genepi, as it is more commonly called in Italy) remained fairly unknown outside its native Europe. The herbal liqueur—made by steeping its same-named plant génépy, aka artemisia, in neutral alcohol—has long been a staple of après-ski traditions, often served neat or simply topped with tonic. Today, as the category continues to grow stateside—including with domestically made expressions—génépy has graduated from alpine obscurity to backbar staple, becoming a popular go-to in cocktails for a hit of herbal complexity without the intensity, or scarcity, of its cousin Chartreuse.

Génépy is not as sweet as yellow Chartreuse, nor as domineering as green, and it adds a cooling complexity to everything from Margaritas to Whiskey Sours to White Negronis. In the Petrichor, Nikki Irvine uses génépy to translate the earthy smell after to rain into a drink, while Toby Maloney describes the Swiss Kiss, which marries gin, génépy and lemon juice and a float of absinthe, as being “as cool and sophisticated as a Swiss diplomat at a party of spies.”

At San Francisco’s ABV, bar staff are known to drink ice-cold génépy topped with a few dashes of Angostura bitters. There, Ryan Fitzgerald blended it into the High Altitude Highball, made with Japanese whisky, namely Hakushu, with génépy and soda water. “Both Hakushu and génépy come from mountain areas—and both are influenced by the region they come from,” he says. 

Finally, the alpine ingredient works well alongside comforting, cozy flavors like coffee and cacao.  “One of my favorite uses for génépy is as a sweetener for heavy cream,” says Troy Sidle, former bartender at New York’s Pouring Ribbons. In the Strong Start, he shakes the two ingredients together with a pinch of salt for a frothy, aromatic topper to the rum-spiked coffee. Ryan Maybee, on the other hand, brings cream and coffee cordial together with the liqueur, crème de cacao and absinthe for the Génépy Suisse. The extra wintry drink channels an elevated, adult mocha. “The sweeter qualities of the cacao and coffee blend beautifully with absinthe, and work equally well with génépy,” he says.

title: Our Favorite Easy Whiskey Cocktails
summary: Go beyond the classic Manhattan and Old-Fashioned with these simple recipes that require just a few ingredients.
content: The whiskey classics—Old-Fashioned to Manhattan—need no introduction. But there are plenty of riffs on those time-tested drinks, along with original cocktails made with the spirit, that deserve a place in your recipe rotation. Here, we’ve collected some of our favorites that are as easy to make as the whiskey staples you know and love. From a two-part rye and damson liqueur drink to a bourbon and fernet favorite, here’s what you should be making this season.

title: Time to Tackle a Cocktail Project
summary: Here's how to master at-home clarification, fermentation, force carbonation and more.
content:
Like any practice, there are levels to at-home bartending. Stocking up on the best tools, spirits for mixing and classic recipes may be one tier of mastery, but building an entire carbonation rig in your kitchen is probably the ultimate home bar flex. If you’ve nailed the easy cocktail projects, it’s time to take things up a notch. Here are five next-level cocktail projects to try.

First employed in the famous Benton’s Old-Fashioned at PDT in 2007, fat-washing has evolved to encompass a whole wave of spirit-infusion techniques. At its simplest, fat-washing requires melting a fat—say, coconut oil or animal fat—infusing it into a spirit, freezing the mixture, then straining out the solids for a bolder, fuller-bodied flavor. Try the technique with coconut oil, chile oil and even peanut butter.

title: Nonalcoholic Amaro Is More Exciting Than Ever
summary: A guide to the growing category with top recommendations from bartenders.
content:
While many nonalcoholic spirits still struggle to accurately channel the flavor and feel of their spirited counterparts, the category of zero-proof amaro has seen promising innovation. 

Without alcohol, it’s still a challenge to address the lack of texture, mouthfeel, brightness or the familiar warmth that’s expected, but amaro has an advantage over other spirits “because you are still able to achieve the familiar flavors coming from macerating traditional amaro ingredients like herbs, botanicals and citrus,” says Robby Dow, owner of Bespoke, an Italian-inspired, all-day café and cocktail bar in Wilmington, North Carolina. For those who don’t drink, Dow says, these spirits present “a very special opportunity for inclusion while still providing a quality product that tastes great.” 

In addition to being enjoyed neat or in N/A drinks, nonalcoholic amari are making their way into spirited drinks, too. “Most people drinking nonalcoholic drinks aren’t necessarily sober; they’re simply looking for alternatives to integrate into their drinking habits,” says Michael Toscano, East Coast Regional Director for The Pathfinder, maker of a bartender beloved N/A product. 

Given the dynamic nature of bittersweet, herbal liqueurs, I’m guilty of stretching open my well-worn bitter umbrella to encompass a wide range when it comes to what makes an amaro, an amaro. But in this case, I’m spotlighting some of my personal picks that would slot well into anywhere a digestif might. Read on to learn more about five nonalcoholic amaro expressions that have my full attention.

title: Beware the Between the Sheets
summary: At Lonnie’s in Brooklyn, the 1930s Cognac sour is a surprising hit with guests.
content:
If you’re thinking of making a Between the Sheets, you might want to proceed with caution. That is, at least according to Patrick Gavin Duffy, who, in his 1934 book The Official Mixer’s Manual, cautions drinkers that the mix of spirits in the cocktail can bring on “sudden intoxication” and “sick headaches.” Bearing that warning in mind, you, like Ryan Gannon, bar director for Ingas Bar and the new restaurant Lonnie’s, might want to revisit this forgotten Cognac classic.

This cocktail first appeared in print in 1929 in Frank Shay’s Drawn from the Wood. It featured gin, Bacardi rum and Cointreau. By the next year, it had traveled across the Atlantic with two crucial changes—swapping out gin in favor of Cognac and the addition of lemon juice—that pushed it into Sidecar territory. The Savoy Cocktail Book inclusion ensured the Between the Sheets’ legacy, and it’s the source from which Gannon first came across the drink 20 years ago. 

Gannon has been tweaking his recipe for the Between the Sheets for the past two decades. He recalls adding a significant measure of lemon and introducing simple syrup (a common practice at the time), approaching it almost like an equal-parts drink. He continued to work on it when he spent eight years working at Cure in New Orleans, where it appeared on the “Cocktails We Love” section of the menu. There, he used El Dorado 3 for the rum and Pierre Ferrand for the Cognac.

Over the years, his tastes have shifted, and so has the nature of bar programs. At Lonnie’s, Gannon relies on a much smaller backbar, so he prioritizes versatile ingredients that can work across the classics and original drinks.

title: The Most Popular Cocktails of August
summary: Here are the drinks that you couldn’t get enough of this month.
content: Punch’s most popular recipes of the month are signaling the end of summer. Whether you’re mourning the sunniest season or excited for the strong, stirred and spiced drinks of fall, these cocktails are excellent transitional pieces, marrying tropical flavors with bitter, deeper tones, for example, or serving the stirred classics, like the Martini, on the rocks. Of course, it’s not fall just yet, so you still have time to sneak in another one of the month’s most popular serves: a frosty, slushy Margarita. Here are the recipes you deemed best in August.

title: Colombia’s Refajo Is Simplicity at Its Finest
summary: The easy-to-make shandy is a staple at backyard barbecues and award-winning bars alike.
content:
On an afternoon so hot that even the breeze had stopped in its tracks, I was already questioning Medellín’s moniker as Colombia’s City of Eternal Spring, just two weeks after relocating there from New York. I squeezed into the singular patch of shade beneath a eucalyptus tree with a friend, languishing on the grass at his farmhouse in the mountains outside of the city. He reached for my hand: “¿Refajémonos?” I grasped at recesses of my decade-plus of Spanish studies and found nothing. Was this some sort of inappropriate propositioning I’d as of yet been spared from? Mercifully, no. I’d just bumped into one of Colombia’s most beloved beverages for the very first time: Refajo.

A beginner bartender’s dream, the Refajo is so simple to assemble that it almost feels too basic to be called a cocktail at all. An ice-cold mixture of light beer and soda, the Refajo is a summertime staple that is far from unique to Colombia. But over the past few decades, the shandy has become so ubiquitous in the drinking culture across the South American country that it has shifted from an object to a verb, à la Google.

“Refajo has been popular in Colombia for at least the past 30 or 40 years,” says Luis R. Vidal, an anthropologist at the Colegio Mayor de Antioquia in Medellín who studies the intersection of food, drinks and culture. It is a clever hangover cure, an ingenious way to extend the beer supply, and a cooling accompaniment for a hot day, all at once. “But more than anything, Refajo is a social drink at its core, one that we associate with large gatherings, celebrations, and spending time together,” says Vidal.

The classic recipe is nothing more than equal parts light beer and Colombiana, an almost cloyingly sweet soda that smacks of citrus and bubblegum and is frequently compared to cream soda, for the North American palate, or Inca Kola, for those who know their way around the South American beverage scene. However, the Refajo isn’t without its regional variations; on Colombia’s Caribbean coast, for example, it is frequently made with a local favorite, Kola Román.

The simplicity of the Refajo gives it legs, and with them the at-home bartender runs. Riffs can involve adding a splash of orange juice, slices of fruit for garnish, a dash of aguardiente for a true kick, or adjusting the beer-to-soda ratio to balance for sweetness.

title: The ’Tinis, All Grown Up
summary: From an Appletini made with green Chartreuse and Suze to a frozen Pornstar Martini, here are six retro cocktails, revamped for the modern drinker.
content:
Ever since the Espresso Martini staged a dramatic return to the limelight a few years ago, the drink has remained a fixture of modern menus. It was the Trojan horse that paved the way for other caffeinated cocktails to make a splash, and it also emboldened the revival (and modernization) of its ’tini siblings. While these kitschy, crowd-pleasing drinks spent several years relegated to Dark-Age-drinks-status, now, thanks to nostalgia and a few modern tweaks, you can have an Appletini at a buzzy new bar and hardly anyone would bat an eye. Here is a look at the ’tinis you know and love, all all grown up.

According to Dale DeGroff, godfather of the modern cocktail revival, the French Martini was “one of the sparks that got the cocktail-as-Martini craze started.” A fruit-forward combination of vodka, pineapple juice and Chambord, the French Martini dates back to 1996 when DeGroff himself debuted the drink at restaurateur Keith McNally’s Pravda, in New York City. It wasn’t until the following year, however, when it hit the menu at McNally’s buzzy Balthazar, that the drink really took off. Though it may be less viral than its siblings, the French Martini, too, is making a comeback.

title: Five Underrated Tequila Cocktails
summary: Go beyond the Margarita, from the Negroni-like Rosita to the tropical Toreador.
content:
In the tequila canon, the immense popularity of the Margarita and Paloma (and their many riffs) has left some other classics overlooked. From spirit-forward drinks to tropical classics and even an unexpected agave-based aperitif, the world of tequila drinks beyond these headliners is vast, and worth exploring. Here are five underrated recipes to start with.

Guadalajara Punch is a regional favorite in Jalisco, Mexico. The large format drink combines various citrus fruits with soda, tequila and salt. It’s served in a clay vessel and is sometimes called the Cazuela Voladora, or “flying casserole”; its easy-drinking nature can “send you flying.” (See also: Cantarito, another tequila classic served in earthenware.)
